mitigation_mechanism: At a watershed scale, soil and water conservation works (zaï and half-moon pits, stone bunds, terraces, cisterns) raise water availability and buffer crop and rangeland productivity against drought. In Ethiopia, a large study of a national land-restoration programme found that in areas that experienced severe drought, programme effects on vegetation greenness and productivity were three times larger than the average programme effect, with increases of 16.71% in a vegetation index and 13.48% in gross primary productivity [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]; buffering effects were also significant under moderate drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_2] and, more weakly, under mild drought [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_3]. Zaï and half-moon pits in Burkina Faso retained soil moisture for 2 to 3 weeks longer, mitigating the impact of dry spells [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. A review of soil and water conservation technologies across multiple countries found they are particularly useful in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3], and a water-harvesting meta-analysis found significantly higher yield gains in seasons with rainfall below 330 millimetres [ev_crop_yield_boum16_4].
caveats: At severe or extreme drought the measured results mostly show no benefit rather than a gain. In Niger, soil and water conservation works could not compensate when 2004 rainfall fell to only 200 to 250 millimetres, and villagers harvested nothing despite the works [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_17]; in Tunisia, four consecutive years of drought from 1998 to 2002 reduced agricultural and pastoral productivity gains and limited soil-conservation benefits [ev_drought_hazard_iegtun13_1]; and a general assessment states that crop yields cannot be sustained during a meteorological drought even where dry spells can be bridged by water-management investment [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Soil and water conservation in Niger raised households' estimated surplus to 70% in good years but still left an estimated 28% deficit in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]. Only one of the units reporting a benefit under this drought cell gives a quantified size of effect [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1]; the rest are qualitative statements of improved resilience, which is part of why the class is capped rather than rated higher. Most of the evidence is from low-income Sahelian and East African countries (Burkina Faso, Niger, Ethiopia), with programme-level evidence also from Tunisia, Brazil and China.

mitigation_mechanism: In-situ water harvesting such as planting basins and ridge reinforcement raises soil infiltration so crops can draw on stored moisture when rains fail. In Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture overall showed no specific impact in mitigating losses from either rainfall shortfalls or surpluses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. mitigation_mechanism: Farm ponds that capture and store runoff let farmers irrigate through dry spells. mitigation_mechanism: Water-harvesting and soil-conservation works slow runoff and spread it before it gathers into floods, giving a moderate reduction in flood impact. In Tunisia, a catchment treated with contour stone walls, terraces and gully structures saw the volume and peaks of average and larger floods fall by about 50% [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_1], with peaks strongly cut and flood times lengthened [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_2, ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_3]. A review of infiltration trenches in mountain areas found they cut runoff by 46.4% on average [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. Stone bunds lower peak runoff at the foot of the slope in Burkina Faso [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1], and terraces on small mountain plots cut runoff and flood peaks [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1]. Check dams cut flooding and peak flow in Iran and held up against strong floods in Italy [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2], and small dams in Morocco damped the damage of serious floods in 2002-2003 [ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1]. Treated ravines in Haiti slowed cyclone floods [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_2], and in India compacted hill terraces limited damage from a major flood and landslides [ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7]. Users of small reservoirs in Ghana name flood control as a benefit [ev_flood_hazard_veno12_1], and practitioner ratings from Burkina Faso, Kenya, Tunisia, Ethiopia, Uzbekistan and Somalia also report less flooding [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1537_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6610_2022_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6715_2023_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6716_2023_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7553_2025_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_flood_impacts].
caveats: Some structures make flooding worse. In Niger, diversion banquettes visibly increased peak flows downstream [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_1]; a review warns that larger sand dams raise the risk of flooding, erosion and seepage [ev_flood_hazard_ritc21_1]; and an expert synthesis warns of serious gullying and larger peak flows when diversion dikes break, about once in 4 to 10 years [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_3]. Strong floods are where the benefit fades: check dams had little effect against extreme floods, especially when badly designed or not maintained [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3]; in Tunisia the volume of large and average floods did not change significantly, only their timing [ev_runoff_reduction_bergaoui00_4, ev_runoff_reduction_bergaoui00_7]; and in Morocco the flood-peak cut held only where floods were not too strong [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_3]. Most of the support is expert statements, second-hand findings and practitioner ratings; the Tunisian catchment is the main measured result. The sub-practices differ: in-field structures do best, runoff-catchment and floodwater-spreading systems are moderate, and terracing evidence conflicts. Much of the benefit falls downstream rather than on the farm that builds the works.

mitigation_mechanism: Terraces and contour stone bunds slow and spread runoff on slopes: terraces lowered mean runoff and flood peaks on small mountain plots, stone bunds lower hillslope peak discharges and in high-rainfall years protect land from rapid flow in heavy rain [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zoug14_2]. In a semi-arid Tunisian catchment treated with dry-stone contour bunds and gully check structures, bundled with bench terraces and a catchment-wide grazing closure, the treatment's conclusion reports flood peaks and volumes falling by about 50% for mean and larger floods, and for the largest (upper-decile) floods peak discharge fell to 60-87% of its pre-treatment level [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_1, ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_3]; a closer reading of the same paper's results table instead finds peak discharges strongly clipped but flood volume decreasing only for the envelope, most-extreme floods on record, with rise and base times nearly doubling [ev_flood_hazard_bergaoui00_2]. Compacted hill terraces with retention walls in Uttarakhand, India are credited with mitigating flood and landslide impact, and WOCAT compilers in Tunisia and Uzbekistan rate flooding as reduced, the Tunisian compiler noting stone lines and walls reduce peak flows during heavy rainfall and the Uzbek compiler that more water is trapped in the catchment [ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6610_2022_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7553_2025_flood_impacts].
caveats: Diversion banquettes and ditches, filed in this family, do the opposite: in Niger they raised peak discharges, and runoff-diversion systems accelerate concentration time with serious gullying risk if the dikes break [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_3]. mitigation_mechanism: Practices that hold water on the cropped field backfire in wet conditions: in wet years stone bunds in Burkina Faso may cause waterlogging in some parts of the field, millet behind stone bunds can suffer waterlogging when monthly rainfall exceeds 200 mm, and in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rainfall exceeds 1 200 mm per year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_waterlogging_hazard_zoug14_1, ev_crop_yield_roose94_3, ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. In southern Africa an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8, ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Biazin et al. cite Jensen et al. (2003) from Tanzania: tied ridges helped maize in years of near-normal (500–600 mm) rainfall, but in wet years (700–900 mm) the maize showed waterlogging effects [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].
caveats: Every unit in the row points the same way, so the practice is rated as worsening waterlogging, but none states how large the loss is or what share of a field is affected, so the strength is not quantified. The harm is tied to wet years, high-rainfall zones or sub-humid sites: it comes from using in-field water-holding practices (pits, basins, mulch, ridges, stone bunds) outside their rainfall window, and says nothing about storage or diversion structures, which have no waterlogging evidence left in this row. The Cameroon observation is unpublished work cited by the authors, and the Burkina Faso statements and the Tanzanian tied-ridge result are cited from earlier studies [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4, ev_crop_yield_roose94_3, ev_waterlogging_hazard_zoug14_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15]. The Ethiopian finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the sub-humid conclusion covers conservation agriculture bundled with reduced tillage [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8, ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. The Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Kenyan losses are held out of the production classes as performance caveats and counted here as waterlogging evidence.

mitigation_mechanism: Flood damages the water-harvesting investment itself by overwhelming or breaching the structure. In Ethiopia, boulder-faced log check dams designed to be more resistant to abrasive flows still had 37.9% fail after a high-magnitude runoff event [ev_check_dam_failure_fran21_2]. On China's Loess Plateau, a single large flood — more than 200 mm of rain — damaged 20% of the main check dams in the Wuding River watershed [ev_climate_shock_shi19_3]. In Tunisia, a project reported the structure copes not well with general river flooding [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1013_2011_general_river_flood].

caveats: The pool is small: apart from the review and the Loess Plateau damage count, it consists of practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets rather than measured damage, and the review ties damage to abandonment as much as to rainfall. mitigation_mechanism: Banquettes lack the capacity to absorb runoff from erosive rains and overflow, diversion channels fill with eroded soil and overflow in the heaviest storms, and torrential rain collapses terrace walls or carries small terraces away in mass movements [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_2, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_2, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_3, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_5]. WOCAT compilers judge radical terraces in Rwanda and contour stone bunds in Niger not to cope well with river floods, while stone-wall terraces in Cabo Verde, stone lines in Tunisia and gradoni orchard terraces in Uzbekistan are judged to cope well [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1553_2012_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1616_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1573_2013_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_6610_2022_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_7553_2025_flash_flood].
caveats: Failure is tied to maintenance and setting: rarely maintained diversion systems generally fail after 4 to 10 years, terrace collapse is linked to abandonment, and the Rwandan mass movement happened on terraces without trees [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_2, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_3, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_5]. The literature hazards are erosive rains, torrential rain and mass movements mapped to flood and come as expert and modelled statements without failure rates, and the WOCAT units are practitioner judgements from technology sheets rather than records of damage [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_2].

mitigation_mechanism: Sediment trapped behind water-harvesting structures slowly fills them, so they lose storage and soak up less water; the damage is real but builds up slowly, so it is rated slight. Sedimentation is described as perhaps the main reason sand dams fail [ev_asset_failure_ritc21_3]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, dams designed to last 30 years were set to fill in 4.4 to 5.7 years [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_1], and 50% of Ethiopian reservoirs studied were on course to lose their useful life before half their design period [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_2]. In Zambia, 8 of 10 reservoirs lost storage to silt and 3 lost over half their capacity [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_4]; 61% of Tigray micro-dams had benefits threatened by silt [ev_climate_shock_gebr18_5]; and in India 31% of earthen dams silted up within five years [ev_erosion_hazard_iegind11_12]. Check dams filled to more than 80% of their capacity within four years in Arizona [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1_av] and fill quickly under heavy sediment loads in China [ev_climate_shock_shi19_4]; small Moroccan hill dams lose 0.5 to 1% of their capacity each year [ev_sediment_retention_roos10_1_av]. mitigation_mechanism: Stone bunds trap the sediment that runoff carries, and that sediment wears down their function: on Tigray cropland, Gebremichael and colleagues found that when the depression behind a bund fills with sediment its trapping efficiency strongly decreases, and considerable soil is still lost, on average 18 t per hectare a year [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av]. The threat is a decline in the service the bund gives, not damage to the bund itself [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av].
caveats: The engine class is low. The row rests on a single Ethiopian study, which states that trapping falls as bunds fill but gives no measured rate for that decline. The study links the decline to lack of regular maintenance and raising of the bunds, so the threat applies to unmaintained bunds [ev_climate_shock_gebr05_3_av]. A claim that pressure on a filled bund leads to structural failure, cited to this study elsewhere, is not in it. mitigation_mechanism: Heavy rain moderately damages terraces and bunds. In China, storms caused widespread damage to terraces, with few local funds for repair [ev_climate_shock_iegchn07_7]. A review of terraces worldwide reports riser collapse and landslides that can grow into debris flows in very heavy storms [ev_climate_shock_arna15_8_av, ev_climate_shock_arna15_9_av], and poorly built vineyard terraces in Spain slid after a single storm [ev_climate_shock_wei16_2_av].
